[[Category:Pseudoscience]]
The '''flat earth movement''' is an organised [[pseudoscience]] campaign insisting the idea that the Earth is flat.

== History ==

[[File:Rowbotham-s-flat-earth-map.jpg|thumbnail|Rowbotham's flat earth map]]
Contemporary flat Earth movement is believed to have began with Samuel Rowbotham, who accused [[classic mechanics]] as a conspiracy to replace religion in his book ''Zetetic Astronomy: The Earth not a Globe'', published in 1865. Later in the US, Charles K. Johnson founded The International Flat Earth Research Society, which attracted 3,500 members by mid-1990s, each paid $25 adhesion fee. Johnson's effort organised the flat earth movement and helped it gain visibility.<ref>{{#cite:Q2980}}</ref>

== Main arguments ==

=== Divine revelation: Earth is flat because god said so ===

<blockquote>
{{#content:Q2982}}
</blockquote>

According to [[Source:Disinformation and Echo Chambers: How Disinformation Circulates on Social Media Through Identity-Driven Controversies (Scholarly article)|name-author]], divine revelation arguments for flat earth capitalises on the identity-driven controversy between believers and non-believers of Christianity. The round earth is framed as an attack on Christian tradition and biblical truth.<ref>{{#cite:Q2980}}</ref>

=== Conspiracy theory ===

<blockquote>
{{#content:Q2983}}
</blockquote>

As [[Source:Disinformation and Echo Chambers: How Disinformation Circulates on Social Media Through Identity-Driven Controversies (Scholarly article)|name-author]] explains, conspiracy theory arguments for flat earth exploits popular distrust in authority, framing the round earth theory as a conspiracy of evil politicians and scientists to hide the truth from the people.<ref>{{#cite:Q2980}}</ref>

=== Naive empiricism ===

<blockquote>
{{#content:Q2984}}
</blockquote>

According to [[Source:Disinformation and Echo Chambers: How Disinformation Circulates on Social Media Through Identity-Driven Controversies (Scholarly article)|name-author]], multiple techniques were used to construct naive empiricism arguments for flat earth. By appealing to people to trust their own eyes, flat earthers reverse the burden of proof of their theory to opponents: prove the direct human experience wrong; and by criticising scientists and framing them as people who think they are smart because they read books and play around with fancy equipments, they also capitalise on the [[intellectual gap]] present in most societies to stir up a people v. arrogant nerds identity-driven controversy.<ref>{{#cite:Q2980}}</ref>

=== Identity work ===

<blockquote>
{{#content:Q2985}}

{{#content:Q2986}}
</blockquote>

Various flat-earth theory proponents position themselves as everyday people who feel lucky having found the truth after long, or visionary scientists like Darwin and Galileo (ironically, both supporters of the round earth) who challenge established dogma. Those identities allow them to justify public ridicule, as the public is victim of a large conspiracy theory and them visionaries are oppressed because they are too much ahead of their time.<ref>{{#cite:Q2980}}</ref>

== Popularity and reach ==

[[File:Flat-Earth-YouTube-Channels-Subscriptions.svg|thumbnail|500px|Although flat earth movement is often ridiculed on, tens of thousands of [[YouTube]] watchers subscribe to flat earth channels.
]]

The age of internet is believed to have significantly boosted the reach of flat earth proponents. Social media and online video platforms provide them with a global audience. In addition, the [[echo chamber]]s created by [[recommendation algorithm]]s help them convince their audience via the [[illusory truth effect]].
